It sets itself apart from the basic algorithm by replacing four binary searches per pixel fragment with an incremental linear search from the previous slice's position, reducing the minimum number of Projection Ray Index (PRI) structures required from three to one for view-aligned slicing [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim is fully supported by the provided evidence. Both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly state that the basic algorithm requires four spline searches per pixel fragment (using binary search), while the proposed method uses an incremental linear search starting from the previous slice's position. Furthermore, both sources confirm that this approach reduces the minimum number of Projection Ray Index (PRI) structures required from three to one for view-aligned slicing.

This establishes the starting point for the incremental search [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the described method establishes the starting point for an incremental search. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports this by stating: 'If the next slice requires a spline segment not used in the previous slice, then a linear search will quickly find the required segment by starting from the segment processed in the previous slice.' It further explains that caching these locations avoids searching from scratch, thereby establishing the previous slice's position as the starting point for the incremental search in the current slice.

This method uses incremental linear search, which is faster when the segment index does not change much between slices [S1, S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the method uses 'incremental linear search' starting from the segment processed in the previous slice. It further explains that this approach leverages the fact that spline segments for the current slice are either the same as or further away from those in the previous slice, implying that the search is efficient (faster) when the segment index does not change significantly (i.e., depth-order coherence). The claim accurately reflects the mechanism and the implied performance benefit described in the text.

An acceleration technique that caches the indices of spline segments used in previous rendering slices to avoid redundant binary searches for the current slice, leveraging depth-order coherence in front-to-back traversal [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the content of the provided evidence. Both Source [S1] and Source [S2] describe an acceleration technique that uses a 2D cache index texture to store spline segment indices from previous rendering slices. This allows the algorithm to perform an incremental linear search starting from the previously processed segment, rather than a redundant binary search from scratch, thereby leveraging the depth-order coherence inherent in front-to-back traversal.
